title: Historic Court Buildings: Derby's dungeons and royal visits

content.content: What's it like to stand inside the oldest magistrates' court in the country?  In this episode, Melissa visits Derby Justice Centre, joined by senior legal advisor Glyn to explore the history of the Shire Hall, built in 1665.
Hear about its origins as a medieval court and public entertainment space, to its links with the Pentrich Martyrs and a hidden underground dungeon.
They also discuss the building's royal connections, its award-winning restoration, and how centuries of history sit alongside modern courtrooms still in use today.
Listen to the latest episode now, available wherever you get your podcasts from!

Buzzsprout
Spotify
A transcript of the podcast is also available.

description: In this episode of Inside HMCTS, Melissa visits Derby Justice Centre, joined by senior legal advisor Glyn to explore the history of the Shire Hall, built in 1665, from its origins as a mediaeval court and public entertainment space to its links with the Pentrich Martyrs and a hidden underground dungeon.

title: We’re hiring in Manchester: build your career with us in software development or delivery management

content.content: Are you in the early stage of your career and looking for an opportunity where you’ll be supported to learn, develop and progress?
We’re recruiting early-career professionals to join our digital teams as Junior Developers and Associate Delivery Managers.
It’s an opportunity to progress fast in an inclusive and collaborative environment, while working on impactful digital projects and services that make a real difference to people’s lives.
You’ll learn through hands-on experience, supported by senior colleagues, mentoring and dedicated learning and development opportunities tailored to your role.
We’re recruiting 10 people across 2 roles based in Manchester:
Applications are open until Sunday, 11 October 2026.
Do work that matters

Our digital teams design, build and run services used by people and communities right across the UK. We’re all about innovation, user-centred design and agile working to solve some of the most important public challenges, and deliver improved outcomes for citizens.
As a Junior Developer, you’ll get hands-on experience working with a mix of technology platforms and a modern tech stack in a Cloud-based environment.
As an Associate Delivery Manager, you’ll help multidisciplinary teams deliver user-centred services, using agile ways of working to solve real problems.

You could work on a great variety of programmes, as well as using AI and emerging technologies to transform how we deliver services. Whatever you work on, you’ll have opportunities to try new things, solve problems and learn from experienced colleagues.
Learn, develop and progress
You don’t need to arrive knowing everything. These roles are designed to give you opportunities to develop your skills and grow professionally.

You’ll have access to learning and development tailored to your role and level. This includes on-the-job learning, mentoring, training and professional certifications, apprenticeships and opportunities to learn from your peers.
You’ll also be part of active Technology or Delivery communities of practice, where colleagues share knowledge, solve problems together and learn from each other.

And your development does not stop with your first role. Working in the Ministry of Housing, Communities and Local Government (MHCLG) Digital as well as being part of the wider Digital and Data profession in government offers a wealth of opportunities to continue developing your skills and explore different career paths as you progress.
Be part of an inclusive team
We want everyone to feel able to contribute, develop and be themselves at work.

You’ll work in small multidisciplinary teams where different experiences and perspectives are valued. We welcome applications from people of all backgrounds and encourage applications from groups that are currently underrepresented in our workforce.

We support a healthy work-life balance with flexible and hybrid working, alongside a range of Civil Service benefits. These include generous annual leave and pension, and up to 6 days of fully paid volunteering leave each year, giving you time to support causes that matter to you.
A chance to meet and get to know each other
Our recruitment process will give you different opportunities to demonstrate your potential and find out whether we’re the right place for you.

If you progress to our assessment centre, you’ll meet friendly people from our digital teams and senior leaders, hear more about our work and learn about the opportunities available to develop your career.
The assessment centre will include a collaborative team challenge, a technical exercise and an interview.
It’s not just about us assessing you. You’ll also be able to ask questions, connect with potential colleagues in your specialism and get a feel for what working here could be like.
Apply now

description: Are you a junior professional looking for a career opportunity where you’ll be supported to learn, develop and progress fast? Join our digital teams as Junior Developer and Associate Delivery Manager in Manchester.

title: Stronger together in rabies diagnostics

content.content: In this blog, we hear from two members of the current rabies team whose careers reflect both the evolution of rabies surveillance and the enduring importance of teamwork, expertise and adaptability.

Their reflections offer a unique insight into the challenges, achievements and unexpected moments that come with protecting animal and human health, while demonstrating why, in rabies diagnostics, we are always stronger together.
Expect the unexpected: a year as Rabies Chief Diagnostician
Charlotte Marsh

When I took on the role of Rabies Chief Diagnostician this year, I knew there would be plenty to keep me busy. What I quickly discovered was that no one can fully prepare you for quite how varied the role can be. Luckily, I joined a team with a huge depth of experience, including colleagues who have spent decades working in rabies diagnostics and have helped shape the service we deliver today.

One of the most significant parts of my role is managing testing for the PETS travel scheme. The scheme involves testing pet serum samples for rabies antibodies, helping to ensure that pets meet the requirements to travel abroad. It might sound straightforward, but there is a lot involved in getting these tests right. Testing more than 17,000 samples last year, while also meeting required turnaround times, means managing the workload can be a challenge.

Another important part of the role is managing the testing for the bat rabies passive surveillance scheme. This long-established project monitors bats in the United Kingdom (UK) for lyssaviruses, a group of viruses that can cause rabies. While I am new to leading this work, I am very aware that I am building on decades of surveillance and expertise developed by those who came before me.

The UK has been free of classical rabies for more than 100 years thanks to the work carried out at APHA, but European bat lyssaviruses (EBLV) have been increasingly detected in UK bats in recent years. As part of the surveillance scheme, we receive more than 1,200 bats each year, with the majority arriving during the summer months when bats are at their most active.

And, of course, not everything that arrives in the laboratory is necessarily what you expect it to be. Alongside the bats, we have received specimens including frogs, squirrels and even insulation foam. One of the things I enjoy most about working in diagnostics is that there is always something new to learn, even if it is first figuring out whether a submission is actually a bat at all!

A small percentage of the bats we receive test positive for EBLV. As rabies is a notifiable disease, it is vital that positive results are identified and reported as quickly as possible, particularly if there is a reported human or animal exposure. This highlights the importance of robust testing, quality assurance and a highly skilled diagnostic team.

I am incredibly lucky to work alongside such an experienced and dedicated group of people. When the pressure is on, everyone pulls together. Whether it is managing the large volume of PETS samples, processing 40 bats a day during the busy summer months, or responding to something much more unexpected, such as testing suspect rabies animals with dubious import documents or confirming rabies in the human case last year, the team steps up. Listening to colleagues talk about the changes they have seen over the years gives me a real appreciation for how much the team has achieved and how its remit has grown.

There is also a huge amount of quality assurance involved in running these tests. It may not always be the most visible part of diagnostic work, but it is absolutely essential. Every stage of the process needs to be robust and reliable, because behind every sample is a decision that can have important consequences for animal and human health.

Looking back over the year, this role has undoubtedly taught me the meaning of "expect the unexpected". No two days are quite the same, and just when you think you know what is coming through the laboratory door, along comes a pile of moss imitating a common pipistrelle.
And now, as another year approaches, I find myself wondering one thing: what will next year have in store for us?
Expect the unexpected: thirty years in the Rabies Team at Weybridge
Lorraine McElhinney

I started work as a Scientific Officer in the Rabies Team in April 1996, before the UK's first case of bat rabies and before the pet travel scheme was introduced. There were six in the team, and our chief diagnostician was shared with the Avian Influenza workgroup. Back then, our team handled the rare suspect human and animal cases and tested only 200 sera a year for imported vaccinated pedigree dogs and cats, a small number of animals that died in quarantine and less than 200 bats per year.

Looking at the work undertaken by the team today, it is remarkable to see how much has changed. Watching colleagues like Charlotte take on the role of Rabies Chief Diagnostician has reminded me how much the service has evolved, while the fundamental purpose of protecting animal and human health has remained the same.

In the past 30 years, I have worked with some amazing scientists through many changes and challenges. The detection of bat rabies in two species of bats in Great Britain led to a five-fold rise in bat submissions, while the growing popularity of international pet travel schemes resulted in a 100-fold increase in pet testing at APHA. We have also responded to the tragic confirmation of human rabies in travellers and expanded our international engagement as World Organisation for Animal Health (WOAH) and World Health Organisation (WHO) international rabies reference laboratories.

One thing that has remained constant throughout those years is the dedication of the people involved. Whether responding to a complex suspect case, a surge in bat submissions or a new challenge nobody has encountered before, the team has always risen to the occasion. It has been incredibly rewarding to see new generations of scientists and diagnosticians bring fresh ideas and enthusiasm while continuing that tradition.

I have also loved the wider connections with other scientists in the Science Directorate at APHA, Veterinary Exotic Notifiable Diseases Unit (VENDU), and imports and border staff. What started as a team of six has grown into a team of 24 staff with a remit to undertake research and testing for rabies and other viral zoonoses.

I feel very privileged to have had such an amazing career in the rabies field at APHA and can certainly echo Charlotte's sentiments that my day job is far from predictable. In fact, despite thirty years of experience, I am still regularly surprised by what each day brings.

Today, I am lucky enough to be in Kruger National Park where two of the team, Megan Golding and Joan Cuesta, will present their rabies PhD research to an international audience. Seeing colleagues share their work on a global stage is a reminder of how far both the team and the science have come.

Building on the team's commitment to innovation and scientific excellence, one area helping to shape the future of rabies diagnostics is artificial intelligence. In the video below, Joan Cuesta shares his research exploring how AI could support and enhance diagnostic approaches, demonstrating how new technologies are helping advance rabies science at APHA and beyond.
Watch the video below to learn more about Joan's work in AI and rabies diagnostics.

Whilst writing this blog, and just after attending an online meeting with other heads of rabies labs, I was joined by a baboon looking for food in my bin. Thirty years later, it seems the lesson is still the same: expect the unexpected.

description: Meet the team behind APHA’s rabies diagnostics this World Rabies Day 2026, and discover the challenges, successes and expertise driving the protection of animal and human health.

title: How TechTrack helped Sophie start a digital career
authors: Jessica May, Assoc. Delivery Manager - TechTrack
Caryl Hodgson, Comms Delivery Manager - TechTrack

content.content: TechTrack is a Level 4 digital apprenticeship programme that helps people develop technical skills through structured learning and practical experience.  We spoke to Sophie Metcalf, one of the first TechTrack software developer apprentices, about changing careers and working in digital government.   Sophie previously worked in education and joined the programme with no prior experience in digital and data. She passed her end-point assessment with a distinction, and has since been promoted to a software developer in the Ministry of Justice.
How has the TechTrack apprenticeship helped you move into a digital role?

The TechTrack apprenticeship has been instrumental in helping me transition into a digital role.   Coming from a background in education with no prior experience or qualifications in development, it has required a big shift in ways of working and has involved learning a whole new technical skill set.   The apprenticeship allowed me to learn the technical skills I need in a hands-on, practical way, directly from experienced professionals.   I have found this such an effective way to learn, allowing me to contribute to projects as I learn.
What has surprised you most about working in a digital role in government?

As this was such a big change for me, I wasn’t sure what to expect when I first started this process, but I have had a very positive experience of working in a digital government team.   I have had a great deal of support from everyone, and I really feel that I have been set up for success from day one. The range of expertise and experience in teams is evident, and I have been lucky to be able to learn from some talented people.
What’s been the most rewarding part of changing careers?

I feel very fortunate that I’ve been able to begin my technical career in the Civil Service, because it has allowed me to be part of an organisation that is making a real difference through the work we’re doing.   I have been able to draw on skills from my previous career such as communication, organisation and problem-solving, applying them in a new context to collaborate effectively with others, manage the workload of being a developer and completing an apprenticeship, and approaching technical challenges.
What kind of real-world impact have you been able to make in your role so far?

I think one of the best things about an apprenticeship is that you are doing the job from almost day one, meaning that I have felt able to add value to my team from early in my placement.   In a relatively short time, I’ve been able to contribute to codebases, adding new features and fixing bugs. I’ve been able to gradually take on more responsibility as my confidence and skills have grown. This has allowed me to make a meaningful difference, while still undertaking my own learning journey.
What 3 words sum up your apprenticeship?

SupportiveI constantly felt encouraged and supported, which improved my confidence and helped make difficult things easier to navigate.  TransformativeCompleting the apprenticeship has changed the way I work, think, and approach my work. It has also given me a career I love and am proud of.  MotivatingIt has inspired me to push myself and take initiative and has helped me prove to myself that I am capable of learning, adapting to, and succeeding in a completely new field.
What would you say to someone considering an apprenticeship in digital?
I would (and have) recommend this apprenticeship to anyone who wants a career in digital. The support, opportunities and learning experiences have been fantastic.

description: Sophie Metcalf explains how a TechTrack apprenticeship helped her move from education into a software development career in government.
